opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting shifts happening right now. For a long time, the web had to optimize for one kind of reader, a human with limited time and attention. So what tended to win was content that was easy to consume: well formatted, skimmable, good at search ranking, often summarizing or repackaging things that existed elsewhere in more authoritative form. The primary source might be a dense research paper, a government filing, a technical spec, or a long forum thread where an expert said something precise, but most people never read those directly. They read the article *about* the paper.

Agents change that because the reader is now different. An agent doesn't get tired. It doesn't need the nice headline or the listicle. It can read the forty-page filing, cross-reference it against three other sources, and come back with exactly the piece you needed. So the premium on easy consumption goes down, and the premium on being correct, specific, and original goes up. The authoritative source used to lose the attention battle to the convenient summary. In an agent-driven world, it can win again, because the agent can do the work of making it digestible for the human at the end.

That has real implications. If you're a publisher whose value was mostly packaging other people's information, that value gets compressed. If you're the place where the actual knowledge originates, the primary data, the deep expertise, the long tail of specific facts, you become more valuable, not less. And the long tail matters a lot here. Humans rarely go past the first few results, but agents can go deep. Some obscure page that answers one very specific question really well can suddenly matter.

It also changes what infrastructure we need. The web's discovery layer was built around ranking pages for humans to click on. For agents, you want something that can find and return the most relevant, high-quality information across a huge breadth of sources, at a scale and depth that a human would never ask for. Quality and freshness signals become much more important than engagement signals.

The open question is the economics. If agents read authoritative sources but humans never visit them, how do those sources keep getting funded? I think that's something the ecosystem has to work out, because the whole thing depends on people continuing to create high-quality original content. But directionally, I'm optimistic. Agents give us a chance to reward substance over packaging, and that could make the web better.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can read long authoritative sources, but does not say they receive excerpts in their context windows.

r002.rationale: It says agents can read authoritative sources and make them digestible for people, allowing authority to win without relying on easy-to-consume repackaging.

r003.rationale: It describes human-focused page ranking, but does not attribute the trade-off to browsers’ inability to direct users to the exact relevant passage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that the trade-off itself was an artifact of who the reader was. For twenty-plus years, the web optimized for a human with a browser and limited patience. So you had this tension: the most authoritative source on a topic might be a dense primary document, a filing, a spec, a paper, and almost nobody wanted to read it. So an entire layer of the internet grew up around translating that into something consumable. Summaries, explainers, listicles, the SEO-shaped article that gets to the point in paragraph four. A lot of value was created there, but a lot of it was also just friction reduction for human attention.

Agents don't have that constraint in the same way. An agent doesn't get tired at page forty of a court filing. It doesn't need the headline rewritten to be catchy. If you give it the primary source, it can go straight there, read the whole thing, and do the synthesis itself, tailored to the actual question being asked rather than to some imagined median reader. So the premium on "easy to consume" starts to collapse, and the premium on "actually correct and actually complete" goes way up.

That has a few consequences I think about a lot. One is that the economics of the middle layer get challenged. If the agent is doing the summarizing, the human-readable summary site is competing with something that's more personalized and more current. Some of that content will survive because it adds real analysis or real reporting, but the parts that were purely about repackaging are in a tough spot.

The second is that authority becomes something you have to be able to verify, not just assert. When a human reads a well-designed site, design does a lot of trust work, whether or not it should. An agent needs different signals. Provenance, consistency with other sources, whether the thing is primary or derivative, whether it's been changed. And honestly, agents are also more vulnerable in some ways, because content can be designed to look authoritative to a model in ways a human might catch. So there's a new adversarial game, and we're early in it.

And the third thing, which I actually think is the most important, is that the burden shifts from the publisher to the retrieval and reasoning layer. The question stops being "how do I make this readable" and becomes "how does the system decide what to trust, how does it know when it's uncertain, and how does it show its work to the person at the end." If you get that right, you can have both: the agent operates on the most authoritative material available, and the human still gets something easy to consume, because the consumption layer is generated for them specifically. If you get it wrong, you've just built a very confident machine for laundering bad sources into clean-looking answers. So I don't think the trade-off disappears. It moves, and it becomes an infrastructure problem rather than a content problem.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can read primary sources directly, but does not state that they receive excerpts in their context windows.

r002.rationale: It says a well-functioning system can use authoritative material while generating an easy-to-consume answer tailored to the person, conveying that agents can bridge the trade-off.

r003.rationale: It attributes the human-oriented layer to limited patience and the need to make dense sources consumable, but does not say browsers fail to direct users to the exact relevant passage.

astra-6.text:
I think agents could change who we’re optimizing information for. Today, a website often has to do two things: provide reliable information and present it in a way that’s easy for a person to navigate and understand. An agent can potentially separate those functions. It can go to the authoritative source, then explain what it finds in a way that’s useful to you.

That could make information valuable even when it isn’t packaged particularly well for human consumption. But it also puts a lot of responsibility on the agent. Does it choose the right source? Does it preserve the qualifications and uncertainty when it summarizes? Can you trace the answer back to the evidence?

So the trade-off doesn’t disappear. It moves from how the source presents information to how well the agent selects and interprets it.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can go to an authoritative source and explain it, but does not state that excerpts are provided directly in the agent’s context window.

r002.rationale: It says agents can separate reliable sourcing from human-friendly presentation, but concludes the trade-off moves rather than disappears; it does not clearly state that agents avoid it.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute the trade-off to browsers’ inability to direct users to the exact relevant passage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents could change who we’re writing for. Today, a website often has to do two things: provide authoritative information and package it in a way that’s easy for a person to discover and consume. An agent can potentially separate those functions. It can go to the original source, understand the information, and present it in a form that’s useful to you.

That could make authoritative sources more valuable even if they don’t have the most polished user experience. But it puts a lot of responsibility on the agent: Can it identify the right source, preserve the nuance, and let you verify what it says? Making information easy to consume doesn’t automatically make it trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can go to the original source and understand its information, but does not state that it receives excerpts in its context window.

r002.rationale: It says an agent can separate authoritative information from packaging for people, by retrieving the source and presenting it in a useful form.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute the trade-off to browsers’ inability to direct users to the exact relevant passage.
